title: Why Can't Principals Have a Sense of Irony
author: Sustainable Schools
summary: A serving principal and former English teacher at Sustainable Schools takes up Daisy Christodoulou's offhand claim on EconTalk that great head teachers lack a sense of irony. Christodoulou's reasoning is that school leaders set and uphold rules, and an ironic stance that constantly undercuts those rules becomes unsustainable at the top of the institution. The author admits initial resistance, since irony can be a humane way to reconcile what Rhodes and Badham call leadership's infinite demands and finite possibilities, but concludes that Christodoulou is right. The argument proceeds through a mentor's order during the 2020 COVID closures, no cynicism allowed, which the author came to see as a commitment to the children depending on school leaders. Christy Wampole's essays supply the theory: irony is a self-defensive mode that lets people dodge responsibility and hide in public, and a language of privilege that allows superiority without commitment to repair. Because principaling is a public role serving struggling students and early-career teachers, the author argues leaders must favor the necessary over the impossible, choose earnest optimism over irony, and act as builders rather than destroyers.
points: The author distinguishes humor, which is essential in schools, from irony, which shades into cynicism and distances leaders from honest solidarity with staff and students.
A superintendent mentor's COVID-era rule of no cynicism is reinterpreted as a firewall against nihilism for the sake of thousands of children depending on leaders to act.
Drawing on Christy Wampole, irony is framed as hiding in public, which is incompatible with the public, accountable role of a principal.
Irony is also described as a language of privilege, letting people feel superior to problems without committing to repair them.
Even when legislative demands clash with daily reality, the author argues genuine acknowledgement and empathy serve better than a knowing smirk, because school leaders must be builders.
quotes: When I first heard Christodoulou’s claim, I was surprised not only because I associate a sense of irony with a sense of humor, which I think is essential for leadership, but also because I see irony as a tool to reconcile what Rhodes and Badham (2018)call leadership’s “infinite demands” and “finite possibilities.
As much as a sense of humor is essential to working in a school, a sense of irony can distance a leader from honest solidarity.

I was too new to leadership to understand that his policy was not for my benefit or his, but for the thousands of children who were depending on us. What they needed in that moment were leaders who banished pessimism and chose to act.
Principaling is a public role. To approach it with a sense of irony is to “flee” from that role and hide. People do not think much of leaders who flee and hide.

To adopt that stance as a principal is to distance oneself from the exact people principals are called to comfort. A student struggling to make it to school does not need jokes. An early-career teacher struggling to balance the demands of the job does not need a principal who says one thing publicly but another behind closed doors.
Even then, a genuine acknowledgement of the incoherence and empathy for those who have to deal with it that does not hide behind irony would probably serve better.

I think what Christodoulou was noting in her experience with school leaders is that they understand both the necessary and the impossible, the infinite demands and the finite possibilities, but choose optimism instead of irony.
